models.best: Inferred from its principle that care is given and returned through kin and neighbours, children could be looked after by many adults who know them, with trust built through exchange rather than fees. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that obligations are built through exchange, families without standing in those networks may receive little care, and the duty to return favours can fall unevenly on relatives. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Mauss, The Gift (1925); Sahlins, Stone Age Economics (1972).

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a family balances its work against its needs, young children could be cared for within the household, at no fee and in step with its labour. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that a household balances its own work against its own needs, a family with few adults or many young children has little spare labour for care, and the principle makes no provision for outside support. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Chayanov, The Theory of Peasant Economy (1925).

models.best: Nursery schools of the New Deal (FERA and WPA), funded from October 1933 under Harry Hopkins, gave children meals, medical care and lessons at no charge to families, and gave work to unemployed adults, which fits a central authority passing goods and work to households. Its figures come from secondary sources and should be checked against archival material, so none is given here.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that a central authority decides what is stored and who receives it, children's care may depend on their parents' standing, and officials and favoured workers may be served first. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Polanyi, The Great Transformation (1944); Polanyi, Arensberg and Pearson, Trade and Market in the Early Empires (1957).

models.best: Inferred from its principle that owners hold an economic interest in the people they own, some basic feeding and shelter of young children could follow, but only as far as the owner's need for their future labour allows. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that enslaved people are denied education and property, children before school would have no claim to learning or land, and their care would be set by owners to serve the labour they extract. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Williams, Capitalism and Slavery (1944).

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a lord owes protection in return for labour, a largely self-supplying manor could keep tenants' children close to home, with shelter and care from the household and the lord's protection. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that peasants owe labour services and rents to the lord, the labour owed takes priority over a household's own needs, so parents may have little time to care for young children. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Bloch, Feudal Society (1939-1940); Capitulare de villis (c. 800).

models.best: Inferred from its principle that guilds regulate training and quality, childminders and teachers trained under statute could give young children care that meets set standards. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that guilds regulate entry and prices, new providers may be kept out and fees kept high, so places may be scarce and costly for families. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Boileau, Le Livre des métiers (c. 1268); Epstein, Freedom and Growth (2000).

models.best: Inferred from its principle that the state aims for a trade surplus and regulates production to that end, public funding of early care could be justified as freeing parents to work in export production. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the state regulates production for a surplus, early care may be funded only as far as it serves that aim, and places in poorer regions or colonies, which yield less surplus, could be the last to be funded. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Mun, England's Treasure by Forraign Trade (1664); Heckscher, Mercantilism (1935).

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a single tax on the rent of land should fund the state, public early-years places could be paid for from land rent alone, without taxes on other incomes. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that only agriculture creates a net product, the work of caring for and teaching young children may be counted as producing nothing new and so get little public money. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Quesnay, Tableau économique (1758); Meek, The Economics of Physiocracy (1962).

models.best: Inferred from its principle that competitive markets and the division of labour create wealth, parents could buy care from competing providers, which may lower prices and widen the choice of hours and places. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the state protects property and contracts and otherwise stays out, standards for safety and learning would rest on what buyers can judge, and families on low incomes may be priced out of care. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Smith, The Wealth of Nations (1776).

models.best: Inferred from its principle that prices carry knowledge spread across many people, the prices parents pay for care would show which hours, places and teaching families value, guiding providers to meet that demand. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that state planning and credit expansion distort production, public planning of places and staff pay could leave some areas short of places while others have empty ones. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Menger, Grundsätze der Volkswirthschaftslehre (1871); Hayek, The Use of Knowledge in Society (1945).

models.best: Inferred from its principle that deregulation and privatisation lower barriers to entry, private nurseries could open quickly, and parents could choose among providers that compete on fees and service. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that controls on markets are cut and the state is smaller, minimum standards for staff, safety and learning may be weaker, and fees may rise where few providers compete. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Friedman, Capitalism and Freedom (1962); Harvey, A Brief History of Neoliberalism (2005).

models.best: Nursery schools of the New Deal (FERA and WPA), funded from October 1933 under Harry Hopkins, charged families nothing and gave meals, medical care, lessons and work to unemployed adults, which fits a model that spends to keep employment high. Its figures come from secondary sources and should be checked against archival material, so none is given here.
models.worst: A 2013 working paper on Quebec's universal childcare at five dollars a day finds durable rises in daycare attendance among one- to four-year-olds, but its authors judged that the costs probably exceeded the returns. These are working papers, and the 2013 study is non-experimental. Source: Lefebvre, Merrigan and Verstraete, CIRPEE working paper 08-23 (2008); CIRPEE working paper 13-34 (2013).

models.best: Sweden's fee cap on preschool and after-school care (maxtaxa) ties parental fees to household income, introduced in stages from 2002, so that families pay in line with what they earn. The enacted amounts are not confirmed by these results, so no figure is given here.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that competitive markets operate within a legal order, care fees may follow the market, and social insurance may not reach care for every family, so some families could pay full market fees. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Müller-Armack, Wirtschaftslenkung und Marktwirtschaft (1947); Erhard, Wohlstand für Alle (1957).

models.best: Sweden's fee cap on preschool and after-school care (maxtaxa) caps parental fees and ties them to household income, introduced in stages from 2002, so that families with lower incomes pay less. The enacted amounts are not confirmed by these results, so no figure is given here.
models.worst: Quebec's universal childcare at five dollars a day, a universal low-fee scheme, was found by a 2008 working paper, using quasi-experimental methods, to have substantially lowered preschoolers' vocabulary test scores, with larger harm for children whose mothers had less schooling. Both are working papers, and the 2013 study is non-experimental. Source: Lefebvre, Merrigan and Verstraete, CIRPEE working paper 08-23 (2008); CIRPEE working paper 13-34 (2013).

models.best: Inferred from its principle that the state directs credit to chosen industries and disciplines firms by their performance, public credit could be steered to build early places, with nurseries that meet set standards keeping public support and weaker ones losing it. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the state directs credit and export targets to chosen industries, early places could be planned around the labour needs of priority industries and judged by output targets rather than children's own progress. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Johnson, MITI and the Japanese Miracle (1982); Amsden, Asia's Next Giant (1989).

models.best: Inferred from its principle that the rent of land should fund public services, public early-years places could be paid for from land values, without taxing labour and capital, and speculation in land would fall. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that land value pays for public services, places could be funded unevenly, with less in areas where land is worth little, so families in low-value areas may get fewer places. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: George, Progress and Poverty (1879).

models.best: Inferred from its principle that cooperative communities replace wage competition, a community could share a nursery and a school among its members, built by example and run without private profit. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that planned associations are built by example, care depends on each community's own resources and goodwill, so families outside an association may have no claim to places. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Owen, A New View of Society (1813); Fourier, Le Nouveau Monde industriel (1829).

models.best: Inferred from its principle that mutual credit at cost lets workers keep the full value of their work, groups of parents could borrow at cost to build and run nurseries, with no rent charged on the buildings. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that free contracts govern all dealings with no state rules, a small nursery's standards and staff pay depend on private bargains, which poorer families may not be able to make on equal terms. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Proudhon, What Is Property? (1840).

models.best: Inferred from its principle that members own and control the firm, with one member one vote, a parent and staff cooperative could set fees, staffing and pay together, sharing any surplus between users and workers. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that each member has one vote, so parent members may outvote staff and fees may be set high or pay kept low, while families outside the membership have no say in the nursery. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Rochdale Society of Equitable Pioneers (1844); Mondragón cooperatives (from 1956).

models.best: Inferred from its principle that goods are shared by need, with no wages and no state, children's care could be shared free at the point of use within federated communes, with contracts replaced by free association. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that there are no wages and no state, care depends on volunteer labour within each commune, so places may be thin where few adults volunteer and families without local ties may get little care. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Kropotkin, The Conquest of Bread (1892).

models.best: Inferred from its principle that trade unions run work through workers' own organisations, childcare staff could bargain their own pay and hours directly, which can help keep staff in post and places open. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that strikes, and eventually a general strike, are the means of change, nurseries and schools could close during disputes, leaving working parents without care for the length of the dispute. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Founding of the French CGT (1895); Pelloutier, Histoire des Bourses du travail (1902).

models.best: Inferred from its principle that municipal and national public enterprise should provide a national minimum of welfare, every child could be guaranteed a public place within reach of home, with fees set publicly and no profit taken. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: In Sweden's fee cap on preschool and after-school care (maxtaxa), the number of municipalities charging fees for all twelve months rose from 69 in 1999 to 181 in 2002, and many said incomplete state compensation justified the change; the enacted amounts are not confirmed by these results. Source: Riksdag written question on evaluating the maxtaxa (2004); Swedish government document on maxtaxa and universal preschool; Riksdag bill from 2000 (proposal figures).

models.best: Inferred from its principle that workers and consumers share control of industry through guild-like councils, parents and staff councils could plan places and hours together, with the state as one partner among several. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the state is one partner among several, a council of workers may put staff interests ahead of the needs of children and parents, and the other partners may be unable to correct it. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Cole, Self-Government in Industry (1917).

models.best: Inferred from its principle that central plans set output and investment, the state could set places, staff and pay for every region together, so that care reaches areas that markets would leave out. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the state mobilises labour for rapid industrialisation, places and staff may follow output targets and labour needs, and parents may have little choice of care. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Kornai, The Socialist System (1992); First Five-Year Plan (1928-1932).

models.best: Inferred from its principle that public ownership works with market prices and managers follow prices, public nurseries could be run to cover their costs, with fees and staffing that match what families and staff need. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that a central board sets the rules and the investment, the board's choices could leave some areas short of places, and managers who follow prices may cut staffing when prices fall. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Lange and Taylor, On the Economic Theory of Socialism (1938; Lange's essays date from 1936-1937); Yugoslav workers' self-management (1950s).

models.best: Inferred from its principle that distribution follows need once classes have gone, care could be provided as a common service, free at the point of use and planned by need, so that each child's place depends on need alone. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the state withers away only after classes disappear, the principle gives no rule for allocating places in the meantime, and need may be judged by those in authority. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Marx, Critique of the Gotha Programme (1875).

models.best: Inferred from its principle that public ownership of key sectors sits alongside markets, public providers could keep fees low in key areas while private providers add places where demand grows, during gradual price reform. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that price reform is gradual and directed by the state, families may face rising fees as prices move toward market levels, and public places may go first to priority areas. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Naughton, The Chinese Economy (2007).

models.best: Inferred from its principle that workers' and consumers' councils plan through repeated proposals, parents and staff could shape places and hours directly, and staff jobs could be balanced in complexity. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that planning runs through repeated rounds of proposals and that neither markets nor central planners allocate, places may respond slowly when a family or an area suddenly needs care. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Albert and Hahnel, Looking Forward (1991).

models.best: Inferred from its principle that employers and unions are organised into state-controlled corporations, care could be funded through employer and union bodies, giving places a steady source of funds. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the state directs industry toward national goals, including war, care and learning could be shaped to national aims, leaving parents little choice and children's own needs little voice. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Italian corporative law (1934); Nazi Four-Year Plan (1936).

models.best: Inferred from its principle that zakat redistributes wealth, zakat funds could help poorer families meet the cost of care, and shared profit-and-risk finance could fund nurseries without charging interest. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that finance shares profit and risk, a nursery seeking funds may find no partner willing to take a share of its risk, so places may be scarce where few investors are available. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Chapra, Towards a Just Monetary System (1985); Founding of the Mit Ghamr savings bank (1963).

models.best: Inferred from its principle that economic life serves well-being, small local centres run on moderate fees and by staff who know each child could give young children steady, attentive care. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that production is small-scale and local, providers may be too small to employ trained staff or run full-day care, so places may be few and uneven between areas. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Schumacher, Buddhist Economics (first published 1966); Schumacher, Small Is Beautiful (1973).

models.best: Inferred from its principle that widespread private property and small enterprise are the norm, small family-run nurseries and childminders owned by those who run them could give local care with a just wage. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that decisions stay with the smallest competent body, small providers may lack the capital or scale to run full provision, so care may be scarce where no small provider can carry it. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Leo XIII, Rerum Novarum (1891); Belloc, The Servile State (1912).

models.best: Inferred from its principle that everyone has a social floor, every child could be guaranteed a basic place and care whatever the growth rate, since the floor does not depend on growth. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that activity stays within planetary limits, places and staff could be capped to save resources, so supply may grow slowly where demand rises. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Daly, Steady-State Economics (1977); Raworth, Doughnut Economics (2017).

models.best: Inferred from its principle that every citizen receives an unconditional income, parents could pay for care from their own income and choose providers without being tied to a job. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the income is unconditional and paid for by taxes on land and natural resources, it may not cover full-time care costs, so parents could still face a choice between paid work and care. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Paine, Agrarian Justice (1797); Van Parijs, Real Freedom for All (1995).

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a government issuing its own currency can fund full employment, public places and the staff to run them could be funded to employ everyone who wants work, with inflation as the limit. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that inflation, not debt, is the real limit, places and staff pay may be squeezed when prices rise, and funding could be cut quickly on inflation grounds. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Kelton, The Deficit Myth (2020).

models.best: Inferred from its principle that communities design, monitor and enforce their own rules, parents and providers sharing a local resource could set and enforce rotas, shared premises and staffing rules nested within wider standards. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that a community designs and enforces its own rules, communities with few members or weak ties may lack the means to run care, and parents outside the community may be shut out. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Ostrom, Governing the Commons (1990).

compromise.summary: A publicly funded place for every child before compulsory school, with fees capped by household income and free for the lowest incomes. Public, non-profit and licensed providers meet national standards, and the state funds the full cost of the cap.
compromise.details: Keeps: income-linked fees from Nordic social democracy (Sweden's fee cap on preschool and after-school care (maxtaxa), enacted amounts unconfirmed), and free places with meals and jobs for unemployed adults from Keynesian welfare capitalism (Nursery schools of the New Deal (FERA and WPA), secondary-source figures to be checked). Blocks: fee rises where state funding falls short, blocked by a fully funded cap; lower language scores and costs above returns, blocked by early-learning standards and a cost review (that evidence comes from working papers, and the 2013 study is non-experimental); exclusion of poor families, blocked by a fee-free place for the lowest incomes. Test: places for children aged two to five, fees relative to income, and language at school entry against a comparison group, over the years after each change. Source: Riksdag written question on evaluating the maxtaxa (2004); CIRPEE working paper 08-23 (2008); CIRPEE working paper 13-34 (2013); Living New Deal, The Crisis of Childcare and the profile of Grace Langdon (secondary web sources); Smith, The Wealth of Nations (1776).
